newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Council renews Haiti force for final 4 months.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Council renews Haiti force for final 4 months.

text.p: The Security Council on Wednesday extended the United Nations military and police force in Haiti for a final four months but cut its size.
The council's resolution, adopted by a 15-0 vote, would reduce the international police force from 300 to 250 and cut the military from 500 to 50 headquarters staff paid for by all U.N. members.

But Canada and Pakistan will again supplement the military force, this time with 650 Canadian soldiers and 350 Pakistanis. They are part of the U.N. operation but paid for by Canada and the United States to meet Chinese and Russian objections to a more costly mission.
China mainly had also protested Haiti's ties with Taiwan, which it considers a renegade province.

Its deputy ambassador, Wang Xuexian, said that although he considered the U.N. mission closed, he supported the measure because of "the urgent request of the Haitian government and the desire of Latin American and Caribbean countries."

Beijing had twice threatened to veto the U.N. military component of the operation in Haiti unless its numbers were reduced, prompting Canada to rescue the mission by paying for its soldiers and later sharing the burden for its troops and those of Pakistan with the United States.

One of the operation's main tasks was to train and monitor Haiti's fledgling police, which replaced the previous paramilitary contingents loyal to the military junta that overthrew elected President Jean-Bertrand Aristide in 1991.

Aristide was restored to power three years later by a U.S.-led 22,000-member multinational force. The United Nations took over peacekeeping in March 1995 with 6,000 troops, a number that has been steadily reduced since then.
But in recent weeks Haitian demonstrators, some of them supporters of Aristide, burned tires and threw rocks at the U.N. peacekeepers, protesting the presence of foreign troops.

A growing number of Haitians are frustrated that the peacekeepers have been ordered not to intervene in Haitian disputes or violence. While Aristide has remained quiet on the issue, his parliamentary supporters have been vocal.
U.S. Ambassador Bill Richardson told reporters he thought the vote was important because the police needed more time to complete training.

He noted concerns about the "internal political dynamics of Haiti which are very dynamic" from Congressman Benjamin Gilman, the Republican chairman of the U.S. House of Representatives International Relations Committee. But he said Gilman supported the extension of the mandate.

Since the previous renewal was billed as the final extension, the Council changed the name of the mission for the third time. The latest name is the U.N. Transition Mission in Haiti or UNTMIH with a mandate expiring on November 30.

Canada's ambassador Richard Fowler told the council that "the next four months will be important ones for Haiti -- its civil police will be assuming full responsibility for all police functions throughout Haiti."
Haiti's economic problems are huge and international aid, particularly from the United States, is less than anticipated.

"The precariousness of the economic situation and the absense of relief machinery are a major problem," said Haiti's ambassador Pierre Lelong. He also said that "the Haitian National Police are not able to meet alone all the challenges which it faces."
